n: This lecture is devoted to forensic biochemistry and immunochemical analysis. The plan has three points: the theoretical basis of the immunochemical rapid analysis method, the theoretical basis of the enzyme immunoassay rapid analysis method, and the use of immunochemical and enzyme immunoassay rapid methods in the analysis of narcotic substances.

First, let us establish what forensic biochemistry studies. Forensic biochemistry studies the post-mortem state and processes of the body, which is why it is called post-mortem analysis. In a short time, on the basis of biochemical investigations, it clarifies the internal state of the body after death. On this basis the exact time and cause of death are determined. This, in turn, helps to establish the cause of the crime.

On the objects of post-mortem analysis. For post-mortem biochemical diagnosis, any biological material can be taken. The most commonly cited are blood, urine and pericardial fluid, as well as material from the liver and muscles. The post-mortem biochemical analysis of blood is based on determining carbohydrates in it. Here attention is paid first of all to the amount of glucose.

Let us consider the relationship between blood glucose and death. In a living body, blood glucose is 3.3-5.5 mmol/l, and after a meal it may rise to 10 mmol/l. After death glucose falls; the reason is anaerobic glycolysis in the erythrocytes. Remember: the amount of glucose in the blood varies according to the cause of death.

t: Glucose and lactate: cause of death
n: Glucose and lactate help to establish the cause of death. In rapid, that is, sudden death, the amount of glucose is lower than in prolonged death. The reason is that the erythrocytes' demand for glucose increases and the reserve in the liver is quickly exhausted. By taking blood from different parts of the body and determining glucose and lactate, it is established whether the cause of death was disease or an external influence. A prolonged agony leads to blood sugar being 20-30 times higher.

The amount of glucose is also determined in the vitreous humour of the eye. In diabetes mellitus the amount of glucose in the vitreous humour may be high. Look at the table: if glucose is high, this indicates pre-mortem hyperglycaemia, that is, diabetes. If glucose is low or absent, the result is not interpreted, because glucose falls at death.

Now we turn to immunoassay. Immunoassay is based on the specific interaction between antigen and antibody. The antigen is the contaminating substance, and the antibody is a protein produced specifically against the substance being determined. The method rests on the specific and highly sensitive immune reaction of the antigen with the antibody. As a result, a complex is formed from the antigen being determined and the specific antibody.

Let us clarify the definition of antibody and antigen. An antibody is a protein belonging to the immunoglobulin class. It is formed in the immune system as a protective function as a result of the entry of a foreign substance, that is, an antigen, into the body. An antigen is a substance that leads to the production of antibodies. Immunoassay is used for diagnosis and analyses in all fields of modern medicine.

The possibilities of immunoassay are broad. The method is of great importance in determining, in very small amounts, hormones, enzymes, neuropeptides, products of the immune system, antigens and others. All products and substances for which antibodies can be obtained can be determined by these methods. At its basis lies the body's defensive reaction: after foreign substances enter, the body starts special, that is, specific, processes aimed at expelling them.

On the immune system and immunogenicity. The system that performs the tasks of expelling foreign substances in the body is called the immune system, and the processes are called immunological processes. The most essential process is the formation of antibodies, that is, special blood proteins, immunoglobulins. The ability of antigens to provoke an immune response is called immunogenicity, and their ability to form a complex with antibodies is called antigenicity. Antigens include pure substances or those of various biological structure, that is, proteins of tissues, cells and viruses, polysaccharides and nucleic acids.

How are antibodies produced? Antibodies are produced by special cells, the B lymphocytes. On the surface of each B lymphocyte there are about 100,000 identical receptors that recognise any foreign antigen. The antigen selects the matching B lymphocyte; this is called selection. The selected cell divides and forms a plasma cell clone, and this clone produces the antibody.

Polyclonal antibodies. Each clone of plasma tissue produces an antibody of homogeneous structure. An antigen in the blood activates many B lymphocytes at the same time. Their receptors have different specificity with respect to the primary antigen. Such an immune response and such antibodies are called polyclonal.

Immunoglobulins belong to the class of proteins containing oligosaccharides, that is, glycoproteins. Despite the diversity of antibodies, they have a common structure, and this structure provides their main functions. Immunoglobulins are divided into five main classes: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM.

The principle of immunoassay and labelling. Immunoassay is based on the interaction between antigen and antibody. In it, one component, that is, the antigen or the antibody, is labelled. As the label, an enzyme, a radionuclide, a fluorescent dye and others are used. The reaction is evaluated on special automated equipment and brought to a standard form.

t: Types of immunoassay: EIA, RIA, immunofluorescent
n: The types of immunoassay depend on the kind of label attached to the component and on the test conditions. If the label is an enzyme, this is enzyme immunoassay, EIA for short. If the label is a radionuclide, it is radioimmunoassay, that is, RIA. If the label is a fluorescent dye, it is immunofluorescent assay. In the table the method and its label are given side by side.

There are two types of immunochemical analysis: direct and indirect methods. In the direct method, antibodies transferred to a solid phase are bound to an enzyme-labelled antigen. In the indirect method, the antigen is transferred to the solid phase and an enzyme-labelled secondary antibody is used. That is, the difference lies in the labelled component and in the structure of the stages.

The differences between the direct and indirect methods. The advantage of the direct method is the small number of stages and the possibility of automating the determination. Its drawback is that the synthesis of enzyme conjugates is not universal and the sensitivity is low. The advantage of the indirect method is the absence of various effects on the catalytic properties of the enzymes.

t: General advantages and disadvantages of immunoassay
n: The general advantages of immunoassay: speed and simplicity of determinations, the possibility of automating many analyses, simple sample preparation, and a high level of accuracy. Moreover, complex and expensive equipment is not required. The disadvantages are a very narrow range of specificity and the influence of matrix components.

t: Immunoassay in screening for narcotic substances
n: Now, immunoassay in screening for narcotic substances. At present, heroin is determined by gas-liquid chromatography, GC-MS and immunobiological methods. Heroin or its metabolites, that is, 6-monoacetylmorphine and morphine, are determined by GC-MS and HPLC-MS. The amounts of these substances are also determined by enzyme immunoassay methods.

The immunochromatographic or lateral flow test is a type of immunoassay based on the antigen-antibody reaction, rapid and performed on the spot, that is, point-of-care. In the competitive lateral flow assay, gold nanoparticles are used as the label, and the result is obtained in about 5 minutes. A point-of-care immunoassay for urine exists. A positive screening result is sent for a confirmatory laboratory method. The results of strip tests are evaluated by comparison with the laboratory immunoassay EMIT and GC-MS.

t: Lateral flow assay for fentanyl: performance
n: Performance of the lateral flow assay for fentanyl. The test detected fentanyl, ≥1 ng/ml, and the main metabolite norfentanyl, ≥10 ng/ml. Urine was tested in 218 patients in the emergency department and in 7 patients with suspected fentanyl poisoning, and the results were compared with LC-MS/MS. In the 218 patients, clinical sensitivity was 100 per cent and specificity 99.5 per cent. The positive and negative predictive values were 92.3 and 100 per cent. At a concentration of 1000 ng/ml of amphetamine, cocaine, morphine, THC, methadone, buprenorphine and naloxone, no cross-reactivity was observed.

t: Test strip reader: visual assessment and digital reading
n: On the test strip reader. The point-of-care strip reader, Uniscan, shows methamphetamine, opiates and marijuana in urine digitally as an approximate concentration. Testing was done on control samples with cutoff added, while clinical samples were compared with EMIT. The 19 discordant results were checked by GC-MS: in 11, Uniscan was correct, and in 8, EMIT. Therefore digital reading is considered preferable to subjective visual assessment.

t: Evaluating the screening result: confirmation and the risk of sample adulteration
n: There are important points in evaluating a screening result. In screening a urine sample, the first analysis is performed by immunoassay, and positives are sent for confirmatory testing. There are three ways of adulterating a urine sample: dilution, adding chemical substances, and substituting another person's urine. Therefore collecting the sample under observation is recommended, and the urine is checked for validity by creatinine and pH. The detection window in urine is wider than in blood, about 1-3 days.

t: The concept of cutoff: screening and confirmation
n: The concept of cutoff. Typical significant concentrations in urine, that is, the cutoff, are given separately for screening and for confirmatory tests. For both tests the substance to be determined and its concentration are indicated separately. The concentrations for a urine sample are given in ng/ml.

Cutoff values, in ng/ml. Amphetamine: screening 1000, confirmation, amphetamine 500. For barbiturates and benzodiazepines the screening and confirmation limit is the same: 200 ng/ml. Cocaine: screening 300, confirmation, benzoylecgonine 150 ng/ml. Compare these values from the table.

The cutoff values continue. Codeine: screening 300, confirmation, codeine and morphine, 300 and 300 ng/ml. Heroin: screening 300, confirmation, morphine 300 and 6-MAM 10 ng/ml. Marijuana: screening 100, 50 and 20, confirmation, 11-nor-9-carboxy-THC 15 ng/ml. The table also gives methadone: screening 300, confirmation, methadone 300.

Cutoff: methamphetamine and phencyclidine. For methamphetamine, screening is 1000, confirmation, methamphetamine 500 and 200 ng/ml. For phencyclidine, screening is 25 and confirmation is also 25 ng/ml. Remember: the screening and confirmation limits are given separately, and both are shown in ng/ml.

t: Forensic chemical significance of blood and urine
n: The forensic chemical significance of blood and urine. Blood is of primary importance in all forensic chemical investigations. Evaluating the amount of a xenobiotic in the blood makes it possible to draw a conclusion about the person's condition or the cause of death. Urine is of special importance: many substances excreted by the kidneys are found in urine in high concentration, unchanged or as metabolites.

Detection times in urine. The table shows the intervals for obtaining a positive result in urine after a single use; the source is CDRH, 1997. Cannabinoids are found after 1-3 hours and are detectable for 1-7 days. Phencyclidine is found after 4-6 hours and is detectable for 7-14 days. Heroin is found after 2-6 hours and is detectable for 24-72 hours. Methamphetamine is found after 4-6 hours and is detectable for 48-72 hours. Cocaine is found after 2-6 hours and is detectable for 48-72 hours.

THC metabolism and elimination, part one. The most widespread form of cannabis abuse is smoking, and sometimes it is also taken orally. THC undergoes extensive metabolism in the body, and less than 1% is excreted unchanged in the urine. With smoking, the initial metabolism takes place in the lungs, and with oral intake in the liver.

THC metabolism and elimination, part two. 72 hours after smoking, about 50% of the inhaled THC has been excreted as metabolites, and the rest accumulates mainly in fatty tissue. Elimination takes place mainly in the urine, 25%, and faeces, 65%. The plasma concentration of THC falls quickly, but the elimination half-life is long, usually more than 20 hours. In an occasional user the metabolite is detectable for 1-3 days, and in a chronic smoker for a week or more after the last use.

Additional biological specimens. With bile, 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives, morphine and other substances are excreted over a wider range. In the vitreous humour, alcohol and most drugs and narcotic substances can be determined. Stomach contents must be taken and preserved in full. Cerebrospinal fluid is the specimen of choice when vitreous humour is not available. In hair, substances accumulate and help to prove or exclude repeated use.

t: Books, qualification data and papers: limits of the sources
n: On the limits of the sources. The book Dvssm gives the theoretical basis of the immunochemical method: antigen, antibody, EIA, the name RIA, direct and indirect methods. The book Gmt briefly mentions immunobiological and EIA methods for heroin and its metabolites. Cutoff and detection times in urine are available only in qualification reference materials. The slides on immunochromatographic tests rely not on books but on abstracts of publications in PubMed, that is, Li 2020, Chang 2012 and Ontario 2006.

We conclude the lecture. Forensic biochemistry is post-mortem analysis: blood, urine, pericardial fluid, first of all glucose. Immunoassay is based on the antigen-antibody reaction; depending on the type of label it is EIA, RIA or immunofluorescent. Immunochromatographic rapid tests give a quick result in screening in about 5 minutes, but the result is compared with the cutoff and confirmed. The screening result is compared with the cutoff, then confirmed with a confirmatory method such as LC-MS/MS or GC-MS. For self-check, revise these points.
